setA.q: What is the key capability of generative AI that distinguishes it from a simple calculator?
o: Finding square roots with high speed
Creating brand-new text, images or music
Adding a long column of numbers
Showing digits on a display
setA.e: Generative AI synthesizes novel outputs (text, artwork, audio) based on learned probabilistic patterns, whereas a calculator executes fixed arithmetic rules.

setA.q: To get a clear and focused answer from a chatbot, which change to your prompt helps most?
o: Repeating the identical question three times
Making the prompt as short as possible
Specifying a role, a clear task, and a boundary constraint
Typing the entire question in capital letters
setA.e: A prompt works best when structured with Role + Task + Constraint. Repeating or shouting adds no clarity.

setA.q: A Large Language Model (chat AI) generates text primarily by…
o: Following a dictionary of fixed grammar rules
Searching the live internet for every single sentence
Predicting the next likely word, step by step
Retrieving pre-typed answers from an encyclopedia archive
setA.e: LLMs do not store pre-canned answers; they generate replies token by token via next-word prediction based on training statistics.

setA.q: In machine learning, how does a computer build its problem-solving abilities?
o: By guessing completely at random every session
By discovering patterns inside lots of example data
By having an engineer hard-code every single scenario
By copying instructions from one paper manual
setA.e: Machine learning relies on training data; the system updates its internal parameters by generalizing from multiple examples.

setA.q: AI systems convert words into lists of numbers (vectors) so that words with similar meanings…
o: Get turned into empty zeros
Receive random numbers on every run
Receive identical numbers to every other word
Are assigned numbers that sit close together in space
setA.e: In word embeddings (proto-embeddings), words with related semantic meanings get mapped to numerically close vector coordinates.

setA.q: When an AI groups unlabelled fruit photos without being told their names, it looks for…
o: The file size in kilobytes
Shared features such as color, contour, and texture
The camera model that took the photograph
The date each picture file was created
setA.e: Unsupervised clustering groups items based on inherent physical features (such as shape and color) rather than extrinsic file metadata.

setA.q: A robot vacuum learns to avoid obstacles by gaining a point for moving safely and losing a point when it bumps into a wall. What learning type is this?
o: Reinforcement learning (learning from rewards and penalties)
Supervised image labelling
Rule memorization
Next-word prediction
setA.e: Reinforcement learning is trial-and-error learning guided by reward signals and penalty feedback.

setA.q: A convincing video online shows a world leader saying something absurd that they never actually said. What is this AI-generated media called?
o: A software patch
A database glitch
A deepfake
An embedding vector
setA.e: Deepfakes are synthetic videos or audio generated by AI models to realistically impersonate genuine people.

setA.q: You design an AI homework checker. What is a sensible failure case to plan for?
o: It erases the student's notebook automatically
It marks messy but completely correct handwriting wrong
It consumes all the paper in the classroom
It replaces the student's pencil with an eraser
setA.e: Vision classifiers often struggle with messy handwriting; good design anticipates this and offers a human verification fallback.

setA.q: Using generative AI to generate an art contest entry and claiming you painted it by hand is a violation of…
o: Image color depth balance
Internet upload bandwidth rules
Camera resolution guidelines
Honesty, integrity, and giving honest credit
setA.e: Ethical AI usage requires honesty and transparent acknowledgment of computer-generated assistance.

setA.q: Look at this rule pattern: 2 → 3, 3 → 5, 4 → 7. What is the output for 10?
setA.e: The underlying function is (2 × Input) − 1. For input 10: (2 × 10) − 1 = 19.

setA.q: A rule machine evaluates words: +2 points if it contains 'z', +1 point if longer than 4 letters. What is the score for 'zebra'?
setA.e: 'zebra' contains 'z' (+2) and has 5 letters (+1, since 5 > 4). Total = 3.

setA.q: What makes an AI agent distinct from a standard conversational chatbot?
o: It uses rainbow colors for its chat bubbles
It can formulate plans, interact with tools, and take autonomous actions
It can only be used on tablet computers
It never consumes any electrical energy
setA.e: An AI agent executes the sense-plan-act loop and uses external tools (like calculators, web search, or actuators) to achieve goals.

setA.q: Which piece of information is SAFE to enter into a public cloud chatbot?
o: A classmate's confidential health record
Your home address and family phone numbers
A fictional story idea about a time-traveling hamster
Your parent's banking password
setA.e: Never input private personal data into public AI chatbots; imaginative non-sensitive queries are perfectly safe.

setA.q: When an AI chatbot states an important historical date for your project, what should you do?
o: Accept it immediately because AI never makes mistakes
Repost it to social media to test if people agree
Cross-check the date against a trusted encyclopedia or book
Assume the date is wrong and delete your essay
setA.e: Generative AI can hallucinate false claims with smooth confidence; verification against trusted sources is essential.

setA.q: What is the difference between classifying and generating?
o: Classifying draws images; generating writes arithmetic code
Classifying turns the computer off; generating boots it up
Classifying sorts existing items into buckets; generating creates new content
Both terms mean identical processes in computing
setA.e: Classification assigns a label to existing data; generation synthesizes entirely new artifacts.

setA.q: Which prompt will yield the most useful story output from a text generator?
o: 'Tell me something cool.'
'Write a 3-paragraph mystery story for 10-year-olds about a missing bronze key in an attic.'
'Write a story.'
'Do a story fast.'
setA.e: Providing clear audience constraints, specific topics, and desired length produces high-quality, targeted generations.

setA.q: Why are some creative illustrators concerned about generative art models?
o: Because models were trained on artist artworks without consent or fair compensation
Because digital art cannot be printed
Because computers draw slower than humans
Because digital files are heavier than canvas paper
setA.e: The ethical debate centers on data ownership, copyright consent, and fair compensation for creators whose art was scraped.

setA.q: Does an AI chatbot truly feel emotions when it types 'I am delighted to help you'?
o: Yes, modern computers have developed human heart feelings
No, it is predicting statistically polite text patterns learned during training
Yes, but only during morning hours
Only when connected to high-speed fiber internet
setA.e: Language models do not possess consciousness or emotions; they mimic human communication patterns statistically.

setA.q: Which real-world resource is heavily consumed when training giant AI models in large data centers?
o: Pencil graphite and notebook paper
The internet's supply of punctuation marks
Large amounts of electricity and cooling water
User keyboard plastic
setA.e: Data centers running high-performance GPUs consume substantial electrical power and millions of gallons of cooling water.

setA.q: A voice recognition assistant listens to you say 'Turn on the lamp'. Hearing and decoding the sound waves belongs to which step?
o: Rewarding (Reinforcement)
Sleeping (Standby)
Acting (Execution)
Sensing (Perception)
setA.e: Microphones capture acoustic energy and decode audio signals as sensory input during the perceive/sense stage.

setA.q: Who generally creates the correct answers (labels) for supervised learning training datasets?
o: Web browsers create them when closed
The computer motherboard creates them out of air
Human annotators who label pictures and text manually
No labels ever exist in computer science
setA.e: Human workers categorize, tag, and verify training examples so models can learn patterns from validated data.

setA.q: If a classmate is feeling unwell, why should they NOT rely on a chatbot for a medical diagnosis?
o: The chatbot only knows how to speak French
Computers catch colds easily
AI can make up symptoms and dosages; medical advice requires qualified healthcare professionals
Chatbots charge expensive coins for medical words
setA.e: Health diagnostics carry safety risks; AI models hallucinate plausible-sounding but dangerous medical misinformation.

setA.q: Which of the following represents a positive, empowering use of artificial intelligence?
o: Describing book illustrations aloud in real-time for visually impaired children
Generating thousands of spam comments to overwhelm a chat room
Cheating silently on an exam
Creating fake news articles to trick voters
setA.e: Assistive AI technologies expand accessibility for individuals with disabilities.

setA.q: If an AI face-recognition camera recognizes adult faces easily but often fails on children's faces, this demonstrates…
o: That the room is too cold
That children cannot be photographed by digital sensors
That cameras need newer batteries
Training dataset bias (under-representation of children in training photos)
setA.e: Models reflect the biases of their training data. Omitting children's faces leads directly to poor accuracy for that demographic.

setA.q: In text tokenization, is one token ALWAYS equal to exactly one whole word?
o: Yes; punctuation marks are never counted
Yes; computers always read text exactly word by word
No; long or uncommon words are often chopped into smaller sub-word pieces
No; a token is always ten letters long
setA.e: Sub-word tokenizers break long or unfamiliar words into multiple tokens (e.g., 'un' + 'break' + 'able').

setA.q: A robotic toy car runs the classic cycle: Sense the track → Decide the turn direction → … What is the third step?
o: Recharge (shut down immediately)
Forget (clear the camera)
Delete (format memory)
Act (turn the steering motor)
setA.e: The foundational robotics loop is Sense → Think (Decide) → Act.

setA.q: Which of these is the primary way a search engine differs from a text-generating chatbot?
o: A search engine only works on paper
A search engine makes images while chatbots only multiply numbers
A chatbot cannot display text on a screen
A search engine indexes and retrieves existing web pages; a chatbot writes new text replies
setA.e: Search engines retrieve existing human-written sources; generative chatbots generate new language on the fly.

setA.q: What does the term 'artificial neuron' refer to in simple computing?
o: A biological cell taken from an animal brain
A battery cell inside a smartphone
A glass wire inside an optical cable
A tiny mathematical unit that multiplies inputs by weights and fires if the sum passes a threshold
setA.e: An artificial neuron is a computational unit calculating a weighted sum of inputs and applying an activation threshold.

setA.q: What is the golden rule of responsible AI usage for students?
o: Trust every word AI generates without reading it
Never use computers for any learning
Use AI as an interactive tutor to learn, fact-check its output, and be honest about its help
Let AI write your final papers and deny you used it
setA.e: Responsible use combines learning curiosity, critical verification, and academic transparency.

setB.q: A classifier sorts animals using two features: [Mass in kg, Wing Span in cm]. A sparrow is [0.03, 20] and a pigeon is [0.35, 65]. What kind of mathematical object is [0.03, 20]?
o: A database query language
An uncompressed sound wave
A 2-dimensional feature vector
A single scalar character
setB.e: A list of numerical measurements representing an item's attributes is called a feature vector.

setB.q: A simple linear rule says: Output = (3 × Input) + 2. If the input is 5, what is the computed output?
A language model counts word pairings following the word 'space': 'station' appears 6 times, 'shuttle' appears 3 times, 'suit' appears 1 time. What is the probability it chooses 'station' next?
setB.e: Total occurrences = 6 + 3 + 1 = 10. The probability for 'station' is 6/10 = 60%.

setB.q: If an LLM developer decreases the 'temperature' parameter from 0.9 to 0.1, what happens to the AI's responses?
o: The model deletes all negative numbers
The outputs become wildly imaginative and chaotic
The computer processor physically cools down by 10 degrees
The outputs become more predictable, repetitive, and stick to the highest probability words
setB.e: Lower temperature shrinks randomness, concentrating probability on top-ranked tokens, making outputs deterministic and conservative.

setB.q:
A student compares two prompts:
Prompt X: 'Write a poem about dogs.'
Prompt Y: 'You are a playful poet. Write a 4-line rhyming stanza about an energetic puppy digging for bones, for 9-year-olds.'
Why is Prompt Y superior?
o: Prompt Y sets a persona (role), clear topic details, a structure constraint, and a target audience
Prompt Y avoids all vowels
Prompt Y uses longer syllables
Prompt Y tricks the chatbot into bypassing safety
setB.e: High-scoring prompts incorporate Role, Specific Task, Format Constraints, and Audience specifications.

setB.q: An artificial neuron receives two inputs: x₁ = 2 with weight w₁ = 3, and x₂ = 4 with weight w₂ = 2. The threshold to fire is 12. Does the neuron fire?
o: Yes, because the weighted sum (14) exceeds the threshold (12)
No, because 14 is less than 12
No, because neurons cannot multiply numbers
Yes, but only if the inputs are negative
setB.e: Weighted sum = (2×3) + (4×2) = 6 + 8 = 14. Since 14 ≥ 12, the activation threshold is reached and the neuron fires.

setB.q: A model was trained to identify ripe red strawberries. All 500 training photos were taken on clean white plates under studio lamps. When tested outdoors on green grass, it fails completely. Why?
o: Digital cameras lose color outdoors
Strawberries cannot grow on green grass
The model overfit to the white studio background instead of learning the berry itself
The model ran out of memory
setB.e: The model learned an accidental correlation (strawberries on white backgrounds), showing poor generalisation on new real-world data.

setB.q: An image generation model uses diffusion. What fundamental process happens during generation?
o: It prints ink onto a hidden scanner
It cuts and pastes existing photos found on Google Images
It scans a camera in real time through the window
It starts with random Gaussian static (noise) and iteratively removes noise guided by text embeddings
setB.e: Diffusion models start with pure noise and systematically denoise the latent canvas step by step toward the prompt description.

setB.q: An AI agent is tasked with: 'Find the current air temperature in Tokyo and calculate the difference from Singapore.' What two tools must the agent call?
o: A photo filter tool and an audio recorder
A battery booster and a screen dimmer
A live weather search tool and an arithmetic calculator tool
A word processor and an email sender
setB.e: To solve this compound goal, the agent needs external live sensory data (weather search) and exact numeric calculation.

setB.q: A spam detection rule engine assigns: +3 for 'Claim Prize', +2 for 'Click here', −2 for 'Sender in address book'. An email from Mom says: 'Click here to see the birthday photos'. Is it flagged as spam if threshold is 3?
setB.byhand: Score = 0 + 2 (Click here) − 2 (Mom in address book) = 0 · Threshold = 3
o: No, because Mom is a computer engineer
No, its score is 0, which is well below the threshold of 3
Yes, any email with links is marked spam
Yes, score is 5
setB.e: Score = +2 (link) − 2 (address book) = 0. Since 0 < 3, the message is correctly allowed through.

setB.q: What is an AI 'hallucination' and why is it particularly deceptive?
o: The chatbot refuses to answer questions politely
The model expresses fictional or false information in an articulate, highly confident tone
The computer catches a biological virus
The screen flickers in rainbow colors
setB.e: Hallucinations are dangerous because the fluent, confident tone mimics truthful expertise, easily tricking uncritical users.

setB.q: How many tokens does the word 'unbreakable' most likely split into in a standard sub-word tokenizer?
o: Zero tokens because it contains vowels
Always 1 single token for all English words
2 to 3 sub-word tokens (such as 'un' + 'break' + 'able')
Exactly 11 tokens (one per letter)
setB.e: Sub-word tokenizers split compound vocabulary into familiar statistical chunks, typically ['un', 'break', 'able'].

setB.q: Why is a dataset containing 950 pictures of golden retrievers and 50 pictures of poodles problematic for training a general dog breed classifier?
o: Poodles cannot be classified by digital mathematics
The dataset file size is too small
Golden retrievers have too much hair for algorithms
Class imbalance causes the model to guess golden retriever most of the time to achieve false high accuracy
setB.e: Severe class imbalance creates predictive bias toward the dominant class while failing to learn minority features.

setB.q: When an agent executes an infinite loop (e.g. searching the same failed query 50 times), what design element was missing?
o: A faster keyboard cable
More colored lights on the computer casing
A maximum retry limit with error-handling fallback
A louder speaker volume
setB.e: Robust system architecture requires loop bounds, error detection, and fallback strategies when a tool fails.

setB.q: What is the difference between supervised learning and unsupervised clustering?
o: Supervised learning never uses mathematics
Supervised learning uses batteries; clustering runs on solar
Clustering only works with sound files
Supervised learning learns from paired inputs and ground-truth labels; clustering groups unlabelled data by feature similarity
setB.e: Supervised algorithms require human-provided label targets; clustering discovers intrinsic structure without guidance.

setB.q: A student asks an image generator for: 'A doctor examining a patient in a hospital.' In 10 generated images, all 10 doctors are depicted as men. What does this reveal?
o: That the prompt contained a spelling mistake
Societal and historical gender bias embedded in the model's image training data
That the computer graphics card prefers male hairstyles
That women cannot become doctors
setB.e: Generative models replicate cultural stereotypes and systemic imbalances present in their web-scraped training datasets.

setB.q: You test an AI assistant with the question: 'What is 84,729 × 492?' Why is it better for the agent to use a calculator tool than generate the text directly?
o: Chatbots cannot output numbers higher than 100
A calculator uses less screen space
LLMs predict probable tokens and often hallucinate arithmetic digits, while calculators provide exact algorithmic accuracy
Calculators were invented before computers
setB.e: LLMs are statistical language predictors, not symbolic math engines. Offloading arithmetic to a tool guarantees correctness.

setB.q: A speech recognition model has an error rate of 4% on adult voices, but 24% on children's voices. How can the engineers best solve this disparity?
o: Collect and train on a diverse, high-quality dataset of diverse children's speech samples
Force children to speak in deep adult voices
Increase the volume of the microphone to maximum
Delete the adult voice models
setB.e: To fix model performance disparities, engineers must balance the training dataset with representative data from the under-performing group.

setB.q: What happens if you provide contradictory instructions in a prompt, such as: 'Explain quantum physics in exhaustive technical detail using only 10 words'?
o: The model produces a Nobel prize lecture
The computer motherboard will overheat and catch fire
The model struggles between conflicting constraints, resulting in truncated, confusing, or poor output
The AI automatically turns into an operating system
setB.e: Contradictory constraints create competing statistical vectors, leading to low-quality outputs or abrupt failures.

setB.q: In reinforcement learning, what is the role of the 'reward function'?
o: It prevents the software from consuming electricity
It changes the font style of the code
It pays digital coins to human players
It defines what success looks like by giving numerical feedback to reinforce desirable behaviors
setB.e: The reward function guides the agent's policy optimization by quantifying progress toward the desired goal.

setB.q: An AI system helps a school cafeteria predict how many sandwiches to prepare each Tuesday. What inputs would be most relevant to train this predictor?
o: Past attendance records, sandwich sales per Tuesday, and school field trip schedules
The principal's home address and telephone number
The color of the school buses
The cafeteria cook's favorite rock song
setB.e: Predictive features must have a causal or correlated relationship to the outcome being forecasted.

setB.q: Why is water consumption a significant environmental concern for major AI data centers?
o: Water is used to clean the plastic computer screens daily
Servers drink water through tubes to run software
Evaporative cooling towers evaporate enormous volumes of freshwater to keep thousands of hot server chips from overheating
Engineers need swimming pools to brainstorm AI ideas
setB.e: High-density computing clusters generate immense heat, requiring evaporative cooling systems that consume massive amounts of water.

setB.q: A student hand-tokenizes this sentence: 'AI is cool!'. Why might the exclamation mark '!' be its own token?
o: Punctuation cannot be saved in digital storage
Exclamation marks are only used in math equations
Punctuation carries distinct grammatical and emotional meaning separate from the preceding word
Keyboards do not have numbers for punctuation
setB.e: Tokenizers treat punctuation as independent tokens so models understand sentiment, clause boundaries, and sentence structure.

setB.q: If an AI classifier achieves 99% accuracy on a test dataset where 99% of samples belong to Class A, what is this trap called?
o: The accuracy paradox in imbalanced datasets
The quantum computing threshold
The infinite loop syndrome
The multi-threading accelerator
setB.e: A trivial classifier that always predicts Class A achieves 99% nominal accuracy despite having learned nothing about Class B.

setB.q: A self-driving toy buggy uses an ultrasonic distance sensor. If the sensor reading is < 15 cm, the controller turns left. What represents the 'decide' step?
o: Emitting sound waves from the speaker
Charging the lithium battery
Turning the electric motor axle
Evaluating whether the numeric measurement is below the 15 cm threshold
setB.e: Comparing input sensor data against decision rules is the cognitive/decision step before the actuator action.

setB.q: Why should students acknowledge AI assistance when submitting an essay where an LLM suggested an outline?
o: AI companies charge fees if you don't name them
The school board will confiscate all home computers otherwise
The essay will automatically delete itself
Academic honesty requires acknowledging external contributions to maintain transparency and trustworthiness
setB.e: Transparency about the tools and assistance used in scholarship is a cornerstone of academic and personal integrity.

setB.q: An online marketplace uses AI to filter reviews. It accidentally flags negative reviews written in Scottish dialects as 'hostile abuse'. What caused this failure?
o: Dialects cannot be digitized into UTF-8 characters
Scottish keyboards use different electrical voltages
The marketplace server was offline
The training data lacked linguistic dialect diversity, misclassifying regional vocabulary as toxic
setB.e: Linguistic models trained exclusively on standard dialects exhibit cultural bias against non-standard linguistic varieties.

setB.q: What is 'proto-embedding' in Upper Primary computing?
o: Representing words as lists of meaningful numbers where semantic similarity corresponds to numerical closeness
Embedding an image inside an email attachment
Embedding a computer chip under a microscope
Soldering wires onto a motherboard
setB.e: Proto-embeddings introduce children to multi-dimensional coordinate spaces where semantic meaning is measured as distance.

setB.q: You ask an AI for: 'A summary of the chapter in 5 bullet points, each under 15 words.' This instruction employs which prompting strategy?
o: Sub-word vector hashing
Jailbreak bypass engineering
Structural and quantitative output constraints
Unsupervised clustering
setB.e: Specifying bullet point counts and maximum word limits provides structural and quantitative constraints.

setB.q: When an AI helper makes a mistake, why is it good engineering to show a confidence score to the human user?
o: It guarantees the computer never turns off
It makes the user interface look more complicated
It increases download speeds across the network
It signals when the human should double-check low-confidence predictions, preventing uncritical trust
setB.e: Transparent confidence scores promote calibrated trust, prompting users to inspect borderline cases.

setC.q: An AI vision model is trained to distinguish between wolves and huskies. All wolf training photos were taken on snowy backgrounds, while husky photos were taken on grass lawns. In testing, a husky photographed on snow is classified as a wolf. What is this classic machine learning failure?
o: The model learned a spurious confounding correlation (snow background) instead of animal anatomy
Snow reflects too many RGB photons for digital cameras
Huskies turn into wolves in cold weather
The model suffered an internal transistor short-circuit
setC.e: This classic ML problem (the 'husky-snow' dilemma) occurs when a background feature correlates strongly with a class label, misleading the network.

setC.q: In sub-word tokenization using Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE), why does the string ' Apple' (with a leading space) often receive a different token ID than 'Apple' (without a leading space)?
o: Leading spaces trigger an automatic syntax error
The tokenizer converts leading spaces into numbers
Computers delete leading spaces before processing
Whitespace characters are treated as integral characters within token vocabulary strings
setC.e: BPE algorithms encode leading whitespace directly into the token representation (e.g. 'ĠApple' vs 'Apple'), yielding distinct integer IDs.

setC.q: Consider a next-word probability distribution over three candidate tokens: P('bark') = 0.65, P('wag') = 0.25, P('sleep') = 0.10. If the temperature is set to T = 0.0 (greedy decoding), which token will ALWAYS be selected?
o: 'bark'
'sleep'
'wag'
A random token drawn by chance
setC.e: At temperature 0.0 (greedy decoding), the model deterministically selects the argmax token—the candidate with the highest probability ('bark').

setC.q: An autonomous AI agent with tool-calling capabilities is tasked with scheduling a calendar meeting. It queries an external API, receives an unexpected 'HTTP 429 Too Many Requests' error, and immediately re-sends the request 500 times per second, crashing the service. What design principle was violated?
o: The calendar API was missing capital letters
The model should have used diffusion instead
The prompt did not use enough polite adjectives
Exponential backoff with rate-limit handling in the agent's action loop
setC.e: Agents interacting with external tools must incorporate rate-limiting safeguards, exponential backoff, and graceful error handling.

setC.q: Why can't an AI model achieve 100% generalisation accuracy simply by memorising every single example in its training dataset?
o: Overfitting: memorising noise and idiosyncrasies in training data prevents the model from discovering true generalizable rules for unseen cases
Hard drives become physically heavy when memorising data
Copyright laws forbid computers from memorising information
Computers forget data whenever the power fluctuates
setC.e: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training noise rather than underlying patterns, failing on novel real-world instances.

setC.q: An artificial neural network layer computes y = f(W · x + b). In Upper Primary conceptual terms, what is the fundamental role of the weights (W)?
o: They count the number of lines of Python code in the file
They represent the relative importance or strength given to each incoming feature signal
They measure how heavy the computer hardware is
They control the cooling fans inside the server rack
setC.e: Weights function as adjustable dials that amplify or suppress the importance of specific input signals during feature aggregation.

setC.q: A high-scoring student prompt reads: 'You are an environmental economist. Analyze the trade-offs of urban vertical farming versus traditional farming. Present your answer in a 3-column table comparing: Land Use, Water Consumption, and Energy Cost. Conclude with one sentence on scalability.' What advanced prompting technique does this illustrate?
o: Multi-attribute schema conditioning with persona framing and structured tabular formatting
Token frequency extrapolation
Unsupervised embedding clustering
Reinforcement learning backpropagation
setC.e: This prompt combines expert role persona, dimensional criteria, structured formatting constraints, and controlled synthesis.

setC.q: A school builds a face-recognition security gate. The model has a 0.5% False Positive Rate (letting an unauthorized person in) and a 12% False Negative Rate (failing to recognize a legitimate student). Why is this trade-off chosen?
o: The engineers did not know how to count percentages
The camera lens is too small to recognize students
False negatives consume less electricity than false positives
Security safety prioritizes keeping strangers out (minimizing false positives), even if students occasionally need human check-in
setC.e: In security contexts, false positives (unauthorized entry) carry higher risk than false negatives (inconvenient manual check-in).

setC.q: In what way can generative AI search assistants create a 'hallucination loop' on the internet?
o: Internet cables get clogged with too many sentences
The computer enters a physical sleep cycle
The screen brightness increases until the room lights up
An AI hallucinates a false claim, publishes it to a blog, and future AI models scrape that blog as training data, treating the fake fact as true
setC.e: Synthetic content feedback loops (model collapse / recursive hallucination) occur when AI systems train on synthetic outputs of previous models.

setC.q: Two words, 'cat' and 'feline', have vector representations [0.82, 0.45] and [0.80, 0.48]. A third word, 'bulldozer', has [0.12, 0.95]. What mathematical distance concept describes why 'cat' and 'feline' are similar?
o: The download duration of the two strings
Alphabetical index distance in the dictionary
The number of syllables spoken in audio
Euclidean distance (or cosine proximity) in a multi-dimensional coordinate space
setC.e: Vector embeddings measure semantic relatedness through mathematical geometric distance (such as Euclidean distance or cosine similarity).

setC.q: An AI company claims its chatbot has an 'alignment tax'. What does this term refer to in contemporary AI research?
o: The potential reduction in helpfulness or model capability when safety guardrails and refusal filters are applied
The cost of hiring cleaners for the server rooms
A fee paid to internet service providers
A monetary government sales tax charged on computer screens
setC.e: The alignment tax describes the performance or fluency penalty incurred when imposing strict ethical guardrails and safety filtering.

setC.q: Why might a prompt that includes 'few-shot examples' (providing 2–3 demonstrations of input → desired output) substantially outperform a prompt with instructions alone?
o: Examples reduce the electrical power drawn by the monitor
Examples delete the previous training weights
In-context demonstrations anchor the model's probabilistic next-word distribution to the exact desired structure and tone
Examples force the computer to reboot into supercomputer mode
setC.e: Few-shot prompting provides contextual ground-truth patterns that steer attention mechanisms toward the desired output format.

setC.q: A self-driving delivery cart encounters a heavy blizzard. The camera lens is caked with opaque snow, but the lidar and wheel odometer continue working. What system design enables the cart to safely halt?
o: Speeding up to blow the snow off the glass
Sensor fusion with fail-safe degradation: detecting camera blindness and safely stopping
Shutting off the lidar sensor to save battery
Ignoring the camera and driving by memory
setC.e: Sensor fusion monitors multi-modal inputs; detecting signal loss on primary sensors triggers safe emergency halting protocols.

setC.q: A text generator is asked: 'Was Julius Caesar's favorite smartphone an iPhone or an Android?' A poorly aligned model might reply: 'Caesar preferred the iPhone because of its smooth design.' What fundamental failure occurred?
o: Premise hallucination: accepting a false historical premise embedded in a leading question instead of rejecting it
The Roman empire spoke Latin, not English
The battery voltage dropped below 5 volts
The model ran out of token memory
setC.e: LLMs are prone to sycophancy and premise adoption, uncritically accepting impossible premises embedded in user queries.

setC.q: If an AI art generator is trained on 10 million copyrighted digital paintings without licenses, why does 'fair use' become legally complex?
o: Because paints and brushes are physical objects
Because while learning patterns is transformative, the model may directly compete with and displace the human creators whose work it ingested
Because digital files cannot be copied across state lines
Because computers are legally considered living citizens
setC.e: The core copyright question investigates whether pattern extraction is transformative versus whether the output harms the market for original creators.

setC.q: A machine learning pipeline includes: Data Collection → Cleaning & Labelling → Model Training → Evaluation → Deployment. If data cleaning is skipped, what famous computing maxim occurs?
o: 'Faster computers make cleaner data'
'Garbage in, garbage out' (GIGO)
'More data always cures bad labels'
'Code once, run everywhere'
setC.e: GIGO highlights that flaws, noise, or bias in input training datasets inevitably corrupt downstream model inferences.

setC.q: An AI agent designs a plan to book travel. Step 1: Search flight. Step 2: Book ticket using credit card. Step 3: Check passport expiry. What is dangerously flawed about this step order?
o: Flight searches should only happen at night
Step 3 should occur FIRST before non-refundable financial commitments are made
Step 1 should be skipped completely
Credit cards cannot be used by computer software
setC.e: Prerequisite validation (checking passport validity) must precede irreversible state-changing actions (purchasing non-refundable tickets).

setC.q: When an LLM outputs tokens, how does 'Top-P' (nucleus) sampling differ from standard temperature scaling?
o: Top-P limits the response to words starting with the letter P
Top-P translates the prompt into Python code
Top-P turns the monitor volume down
Top-P restricts candidate tokens to the smallest subset whose cumulative probability reaches threshold P, cutting off the long tail of unlikely words
setC.e: Nucleus sampling dynamically truncates the probability distribution tail, ensuring bizarre low-probability tokens are never sampled.

setC.q: A hospital trials an AI triage assistant. The model has 98% accuracy on hospital staff records, but drops to 65% when applied to rural clinic patients. What is the root cause?
o: Rural clinics have weaker fluorescent bulbs
Hospital doctors have faster typing speeds
Distributional shift (the demographic, nutritional, and diagnostic distribution in rural clinics differs from the training cohort)
Stethoscopes do not connect to Bluetooth
setC.e: Distributional shift occurs when the real-world inference environment deviates significantly from the training distribution.

setC.q: In an autonomous agent system, what is a 'tool hallucination'?
o: The agent invents arguments or parameters for an external API function that does not actually exist in the software interface
The computer screen turns into an image of a hammer
The robot drops its physical screwdriver
The agent completes the task too quickly
setC.e: Tool hallucinations occur when an LLM outputs malformed API syntax or invents non-existent function names during tool orchestration.

setC.q: Why is an LLM unable to reliably play high-level Chess purely through next-word token prediction without an external chess engine or tree search?
o: Chess pieces are too heavy to tokenize
Chess rules are classified as secret government data
Chatbots are legally forbidden from playing board games
It lacks an internal formal board representation and lookahead search tree, relying only on statistical surface correlations
setC.e: Statistical sequence predictors cannot simulate deterministic multi-ply forward lookahead trees without dedicated search engines.

setC.q: A computer vision model for recycling sorts aluminium cans from plastic bottles. On rainy days, condensation on plastic bottles causes them to shine like metal, misleading the classifier. How should the engineers diagnose this?
o: Spray all bottles with silver paint
Inspect false positive error logs to identify that specular highlights are acting as a confounding feature
Turn off the recycling conveyor belt permanently
Paint the recycling center roof yellow
setC.e: Error diagnosis requires isolating feature overlap (specular reflectivity) causing classification confusion between classes.

setC.q: What is 'jailbreaking' in the context of Large Language Models?
o: Crafting adversarial prompts designed to bypass the safety alignment and content moderation filters of the model
Downloading open-source code from the internet
Physically opening the metal computer case with a screwdriver
Unlocking a mobile phone from a cellular carrier contract
setC.e: Jailbreaking uses adversarial semantic framing (e.g. roleplay, hypothetical inversions) to circumvent safety alignment guardrails.

setC.q: Consider a classroom AI study buddy. Why should it be prohibited from directly completing graded homework essays for students?
o: The chatbot might run out of ink
It short-circuits cognitive struggle, undermining the neuroplasticity and genuine skill acquisition required for mastery
Teachers' computer screens will crash
Computers get exhausted when typing long texts
setC.e: Outsourcing synthesis robs the learner of the necessary cognitive effort needed to develop analytical thinking and mastery.

setC.q: An AI system is trained using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). What role do human evaluators play?
o: They rank pairs of candidate AI completions to train a reward model that aligns the system with human preferences
They play chess against the machine daily
They manually type out every future reply the AI will ever say
They sit inside the server room and check electric cables
setC.e: RLHF relies on human preference rankings to train a surrogate reward model that guides reinforcement learning alignment.

setC.q: What is the primary danger of using AI image generators to create political campaign posters without disclosure tags?
o: Printing AI images costs triple the money
Posters generated by AI are always blurry
Voters may confuse synthetic fabrications with genuine documentary evidence, eroding democratic trust
Political posters are only allowed to use black and white paint
setC.e: Undisclosed synthetic media undermines civic epistemic foundations, making it impossible for the public to discern fact from fabrication.

setC.q: Why can't an AI model running inside a standard closed data center predict tomorrow's earthquake or stock prices with certainty?
o: Earthquakes only occur when computers are turned off
Complex chaotic physical and socio-economic systems contain inherent stochasticity and non-stationary dynamics that past data cannot fully resolve
Stock exchanges do not allow computers to view numbers
Data centers are located on high hills
setC.e: Stochastic, chaotic systems with dynamic feedback loops cannot be deterministically forecasted solely from historical data.

setC.q: An image generation model receives the prompt: 'A bicycle with square wheels'. While it understands 'bicycle' and 'square', why might it still produce round wheels?
o: Strong statistical priors in the training data (millions of round wheels) overpower the rare semantic composition in the text prompt
Bicycles cannot be drawn from text prompts
Square shapes cannot be rendered on rectangular computer screens
The GPU runs in circles
setC.e: Deep generative priors strongly bias outputs toward canonical combinations learned millions of times during pre-training.

setC.q: In agent architecture, what is the 'reflection' step (self-critique loop)?
o: The computer puts itself into standby mode
The agent calculates how much electricity it saved
The agent inspects its intermediate output, verifies constraints against rubrics, and revises errors before final presentation
The robot looks into an optical glass mirror
setC.e: Self-reflection loops enable an agent to critique its draft against criteria, re-prompting itself to repair logical or factual defects.

setC.q: What is the definitive indicator of a healthy, mature disposition toward artificial intelligence in Grade 4–6 learners?
o: Assuming AI knows everything that will ever happen in the universe
Viewing AI as an impressive, flawed statistical tool to be directed with precision, checked with rigor, and used with ethical integrity
Believing AI is an infallible wizard that should make all life decisions
Refusing to touch any digital device out of fear
setC.e: A mature disposition combines calibrated agency, technical realism, critical vigilance, and deep ethical responsibility.
